chunks.text: Harness-Driven Agentic Operation of Optical Pooled Screen Analysis An approach to automating and maintaining computational biology pipelines Matteo Di Bernardo1,2 Claire Peterson3 Ege Topkoc4,1 Matt Might3 Iain M. Cheeseman1,2 1Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research, Cambridge, MA, USA 2Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, USA 3Precision Medicine Institute, University of Alabama at Birmingham, AL, USA 4Boston University, Boston, MA, USA matteo.dibernardo@gmail.com, icheese@wi.mit.edu Abstract Optical pooled screens connect genetic perturbations to changes in cell morphol- ogy and behavior, but turning the microscopy data into interpretable results takes complex, multi-day analyses. Established pipelines process this data, yet re- searchers still select parameters, inspect outputs, and resolve failures for each experiment. Here, we present Brieflow-auto, a pipeline-specific harness imple- mented as a Claude Code plugin that lets a coding large language model (LLM) operate Brieflow, an open-source end-to-end pipeline for optical pooled screen- ing data. A researcher supplies experimental facts and approves the launch. An agent tunes parameters in an interactive notebook, and the harness validates the configuration, monitors execution, recovers from common failures, and checks output quality. For pipeline defects, the agent opens upstream issues proposing backward-compatible fixes for the broader community. In five previously analyzed screens, harness runs yielded more cells with a confident single-gene assignment than the original hand analyses. On a screen the pipeline was not designed for, the harness turned each failure into a reviewed upstream fix. More broadly, we propose that wrapping an established pipeline in a harness can substantially accelerate its use and the long-term reliability of its codebase.

1 Introduction Understanding how genes shape cell behavior requires measuring the consequences of genetic pertur- bations. Optical pooled screening (OPS) combines pooled genetic perturbations with microscopy, using an in situ barcode readout to link each cell’s appearance to its perturbation [Feldman et al., 2019, Di Bernardo et al., 2026]. Unlike screens read out by sequencing, OPS requires extracting cellular features from terabytes of images and matching them to perturbation identities, a multi-day analysis that demands expertise in parameter selection, image inspection, and troubleshooting. AI agents now support scientific analyses in several ways. Discovery platforms such as Biomni and Kosmos coordinate analyses across many tools and have led to experimentally validated discover- ies [Huang et al., 2025, Mitchener et al., 2025]. Coding agents can also apply established tools under expert guidance. In a recent Anthropic report, Claude autonomously ran de novo protein binder design campaigns from a single protocol prompt and produced confirmed binders against 14 of 15 testable targets [Claude Science and Shanehsazzadeh, 2026]. Companies such as Tamarind make complex protein-design tools accessible to researchers as a service with a user interface [Tamarind Bio, 2026]. However, many laboratories and core facilities already have an established analysis pipeline, and their main cost is running it for each new experiment. For these groups, the analysis itself should stay fixed while an agent handles configuration, execution, and recovery from failures. This requires reliable execution and software that can be maintained across experiments, both of which remain 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: Agentic Life Sciences.

Blue is agent judgment, white a scripted step, orange researcher input or review, and grey a record. challenging for agents on benchmarks of computational reproduction and iterative coding [Siegel et al., 2024, Orlanski et al., 2026]. Building a dedicated service for each pipeline is also a substantial commitment for an academic laboratory or core. Here, we present Brieflow-auto, a harness that lets a coding large language model (LLM) operate Brieflow, an open-source end-to-end pipeline for large-scale OPS microscopy data [Di Bernardo et al., 2026]. The harness encodes our experience with the pipeline and its failure modes in a Claude Code plugin. It records run state and requires the researcher’s approval before launch, after which the agent handles tuning and most operating decisions without changing pipeline code. Defects become upstream issues with backward-compatible fixes, so the codebase evolves through review rather than through edits made during a run. We hypothesize that separating routine operation from pipeline development reduces manual work while preserving a reproducible, maintainable codebase.

We describe the changes to Brieflow that enabled agent use, test the harness on five previously analyzed screens and on a screen outside the pipeline’s original use, and release the plugin with an adaptation guide for other groups’ pipelines. 2 Brieflow OPS analysis must connect barcode identities with measurements of the same cells, combining multi- cycle sequencing-by-synthesis (SBS) images with phenotype imaging. Brieflow [Di Bernardo et al., 2026] established an integrated workflow from raw microscope files through barcode assignment and phenotyping to interpretable groups of perturbations. Running it still requires configuring each stage, inspecting representative images, and troubleshooting failures, which limits access for experimental biologists and costs experienced users time. Brieflow’s Snakemake [Mölder et al., 2021] directed acyclic graph (DAG) provides two properties a harness needs. Failed jobs resume without repeating completed work, so a tile that runs out of memory is retried without restarting a multi-day analysis, and the graph is divided into seven modules (preprocess, SBS, phenotype, merge, classify, aggregate, and cluster) whose boundaries are checkpoints for quality checks and human intervention. While Brieflow holds the library functions and module rules, each screen has a separate analysis repository containing its notebooks, configuration, and a fixed reference to the pipeline version used. This separation lets the harness configure each screen independently of the shared pipeline code. Three infrastructure changes made Brieflow practical to run at scale through an agent. We converted output image formats to chunked, cloud-ready OME-Zarr [Moore et al., 2021, Miles and Zarr Developers, 2025] and tables to Polars [Vink and Polars Developers, 2026], removing per-tile read and conversion overhead.

In our benchmarks against tiled TIFF, OME-Zarr gave a median 1.5-fold speedup and 21 percent lower peak memory with concordant feature outputs, and the advantage widened under concurrency, which made running several screens on one machine practical. We adapted the Jupyter configuration notebooks, whose hidden execution state and hard-to-read file changes make them difficult for agents to edit reliably, as marimo [marimo team, 2026] notebooks: plain Python with explicit cell dependencies, so changing a parameter invalidates only dependent 2 cells and the harness tunes the same notebook the researcher reads. Finally, we gave the module entry points one shared interface for running a module or the full sequence. The largest challenge in OPS analysis is that screens vary in cell density and morphology, microscope format and metadata, barcode length and chemistry, and phenotype panels. Brieflow exposes parameters for these differences, and we added a structured experiment description in which the researcher records them once, before launching an analysis. Together, these changes let the harness work within a small screen repository with a declared pipeline version, and refer defects found during a run back to pipeline development. 3 Brieflow-auto Brieflow-auto implements a pipeline-specific harness as a Claude Code plugin [Anthropic, 2026a]. Claude Code supplies the runtime, while Brieflow-auto supplies the operating instructions, tools, and policies (Figure 1). This use of harness follows work on structured support for long-running agents [Young, 2025]. The researcher supplies experimental facts and approves launch, while the agent inspects data and tunes parameters within developer-defined ranges. When a required fact is missing, the harness asks the researcher. The protocol prohibits changing pipeline code or quality thresholds during a run, keeping the scientific method and acceptance criteria under researcher control.

Importantly, a written operating guide alone would not suffice. In our experience, agent runs failed mainly when the agent lost track of the run’s state rather than for lack of instructions. We therefore implemented each state check, such as whether a module is complete, whether a value is accepted, and whether a job may resume, as a script that the harness runs rather than as written guidance. Brieflow-auto analyzes one screen at a time, and it configures, validates, runs, and checks each of the screen’s modules in turn. Once the agent has selected parameters, the harness checks them against the pipeline’s requirements before launching work, then monitors execution and evaluates the outputs against established quality criteria. A known operational failure triggers a prescribed, bounded recovery, such as raising memory and resuming a failed job without repeating completed work. An unknown failure or a failed quality check pauses for review. Parameters, their sources, decisions, and completed stages are recorded alongside the analysis, so a run can resume after an interruption without relying on the agent’s earlier conversation. Although the agent can address some errors and issues as they arise, some problems require changes to the pipeline itself. For an identified defect, the agent opens an upstream issue with shareable failure evidence, run context, and a proposed backward-compatible fix. The proposed change must preserve the existing behavior and capabilities of the overall pipeline, not reshape the pipeline for one screen. Brieflow’s maintainers, the developers who review and merge changes to its code, then review and release fixes for later analyses, as illustrated in Section 4.3. The harness also records each run and, with the researcher’s consent, the agent’s transcripts, so that proposed improvements to the harness itself can be tied to evidence from real runs (Section E).

4 Deployment 4.1 Interview and run To initiate Brieflow-auto, the researcher first asks the coding agent to configure an analysis and answers an interview about the experiment. The harness fills parameters from that description, established defaults, and data inspection, asking only where information is missing. On the two reanalyses whose interview records survive, 6 and 9 of the 212 resolved variables were questions put to the researcher, who supplied 14 and 12 values in total (Figure 5). The researcher then reviews the resolved plan and approves the launch. From there, Brieflow-auto enters its run loop and works through the screen one module at a time. For each module, the agent parametrizes and tunes the module’s notebook, and the harness validates, runs, and checks it before moving to the next. The harness notifies the researcher as the run progresses and stops only when a failure or a quality check needs a decision. Sections C and D illustrate the interview and the run loop. 4.2 Rerunning existing screens To evaluate Brieflow-auto, we reran five previously analyzed screens and compared agent-driven operation with the original manual analyses, a test of whether the harness preserves analysis quality while reducing the work of configuring and supervising the pipeline. A critical element of analyzing OPS data is the tuning of parameters that control barcode assignment, which are inherently difficult to optimize over one tile of data and require sweeping over a number of individual levers. Compared with the hand analyses, the harness runs yielded 3.8 to 39.2 percent more cells with a confident single-gene assignment at the end of merge, in all five pairs and from the same raw images. The agent re-tuned the SBS peak threshold and the segmentation diameters for each screen. Base calling and barcode assignment used the same code as the hand analyses. Where both analyses recorded it, the SBS mapping rate also rose, so the additional reads matched the library rather than adding unmapped noise. The share of cells entering aggregation that carry such an assignment also increased in four of the five pairs (Figure 2, Table 1). Higher counts measure yield, not assignment accuracy. 4.3 Extending the pipeline’s reach After the reanalyses, we tested whether the harness could extend Brieflow to a screen it was not designed for. We applied Brieflow-auto to a drug screen from another laboratory. As in a knockout screen, each cell carries an in situ sequenced barcode and is imaged for its phenotype. However, the barcodes identify constructs rather than knockouts, and each construct is scored under treatment against its own untreated arm. The screen was also imaged on a microscope whose file format and well names Brieflow did not yet support, and it used a two-color sequencing chemistry in which one base carries no dye. When a module failed, the harness classified the failure and reported it with the error and the context of the run, and each problem led to a pull request with a backward-compatible fix (Section G). For the microscope, the agent identified the metadata and well names that the pipeline needed to read.

For the two-color chemistry, it traced reads that failed to map back to how bases were called and proposed a base caller suited to the chemistry. For the drug design, it proposed changes to how constructs are grouped and compared with their untreated arm. Importantly, these proposals did not always fit the pipeline’s code organization, and the Brieflow maintainers adapted them before merging. Together, these changes extended Brieflow from knockout screens to drug screens of barcoded constructs within one maintained pipeline. 5 Conclusions Brieflow-auto demonstrates how a coding agent can operate an established pipeline through explicit configuration, checks, and records. On five different screens, Brieflow-auto yielded more usable cells than the hand analyses it replaced, and on a screen outside the pipeline’s original use each failure led to a reviewed upstream fix instead of an unreviewed change during the run. This implementation is narrow, but it addresses a difficult, long-running analysis with many ways to fail. Many other biological pipelines share these failure modes and the module boundaries that a harness needs. We therefore expect that a similar harness can be built for them, and we provide an adaptation guide as a starting point. Broader paired runs with precision checks, time measurements, and ablations that separate the harness from pipeline changes would test these claims more directly. Data and code availability The harness is at https://github.com/cheeseman-lab/brieflow-auto (plugin, HARNESS.md). The pipeline is at https://github.com/cheeseman-lab/brieflow. Both are in active development and will change after publication. The per-screen tables and figure sources, decision journals, run manifests, and notebook exports are available on request. A Setup and runtime A setup process transfers the data and prepares the runtime environment on the machine that executes the analysis, which can be remote or local. We provide a Slurm backend for HPC runs and a local backend for Google Cloud runs, and these can readily be extended to other compute backends. Claude Code, the notebook tools, the software environment, and the runner all reside on the execution machine. The researcher works in a terminal session on that machine, which stays open if the connection drops. Claude Code Remote Control [Anthropic, 2026b] lets the researcher follow a run from another device, and Brieflow-auto sends progress alerts to Slack. B Input data The harness takes three inputs, and the researcher supplies all of them before the interview. The first is the raw imaging data: the multi-cycle SBS images and the phenotype images, staged under one directory per screen. Setup validates this tree against the layout the pipeline expects, with sequencing cycles and phenotype rounds under each plate, and converts common alternative layouts. It reports a missing cycle or plate as a blocker instead of guessing. The second is the barcode library file, the design table that maps each barcode sequence to its gene.

The third is screen.yaml, a structured description of the experiment that the researcher writes once. It records the perturbation library (vector, barcode columns and lengths, DNA or RNA detection target, controls), the SBS acquisition (cycle count, chemistry, channels and base order), the phenotype acquisition (one entry per channel with its marker), and the cell type and growth conditions. C Interview The interview runs once, after the data are staged and setup is complete, and resolves the parameters of every module before any compute is spent. It separates experimental facts from values that can be resolved without another question. The agent asks about unresolved facts, then tunes image-dependent parameters on representative data. Each value is stored with its source (Figure 3). The run starts only after the researcher approves the launch review. 6 agent scripted researcher records experiment ledger (screen.yaml) lab defaults data probes researcher answers Agent: “Segmentation method: cellpose or stardist?” Researcher: “cellpose.” launch review every value with its source gaps still to answer resources and sweeps planned approve run starts Figure 3: Several sources resolve every parameter into one launch review, and only the values no source can supply become questions for the researcher. The review states each value with its source, the gaps, and the planned resources before the researcher approves and the run starts. Colors follow Figure 1. D Run loop The harness drives the pipeline’s modules through one entry point, bin/brieflow-run, which steps through an ordered list of modules and their notebooks. Adding or reordering a module means editing that list. Flags on the runner choose which modules to run and whether jobs go to a Slurm cluster or run on the local machine, so the same command works on a cluster, a workstation, or a cloud virtual machine. Every module goes through the same four steps, configure, validate, run, and check (Figure 4).

First, the agent configures the module. It fills the module’s notebook from the interview and sweeps the tunable parameters in a live marimo kernel, so each trial recomputes only the cells downstream of the changed value. Second, a preflight check compares the resulting configuration against the pipeline’s code and rejects values that the pipeline would fail on, within seconds rather than after hours of cluster time. Third, a monitor runs the module. It watches the jobs, classifies any failure, raises memory and resumes after an out-of-memory error, waits and resumes after filesystem delays, raises the open-file limit when jobs run out of file handles, and stops the run for any other failure. Finally, a quality gate reads the module’s metrics from the pipeline’s own evaluation outputs and compares them against set thresholds. agent scripted researcher records configure validate run check next module interview record → notebook, config config vs pipeline rules logs, resume state QC summary vs policy researcher can open and run the notebook known failure: raise memory, or wait, then resume preflight finding stop gate failed stop unrecovered stop pipeline defect →escalate Figure 4: Every module passes the same cycle, and each step reads and writes a record. The researcher and the agent work in the same notebook. The researcher can open and run any module’s notebook, stop a sweep, change values, and inspect the resulting images, then hand control back once the changes have been recorded and validated. 7 E Harness details Records. Everything the harness resolves or decides is written to files stored with the screen.

These include each parameter and where its value came from (the researcher, the screen description, a lab default, a data probe, or a sweep), the versions of the harness and pipeline used, and any issues the agent opened. Important choices also go to a decision journal that marks each as automatic, an agent judgment, or a researcher decision. For example, a bounded memory increase is recorded as automatic, a choice between two parameter candidates as agent judgment, and launch approval as a researcher decision. Another researcher can read these files back to see how a result was produced. Escalation. The runner saves failure evidence locally. The agent investigates pipeline defects and opens GitHub issues through /brieflow-issue, following Brieflow’s reporting template. Each report includes a proposed backward-compatible fix. The agent checks for duplicates and removes private data before submission, and the helper records the issue URL. Agent boundary. The runtime agent can inspect inputs, logs, metrics and images, and set parameters within the ranges in the defaults file. It can write config and run artifacts, launch, resume, recover or pause through the provided scripts, and record decisions and findings. It cannot edit pipeline source during a run, change quality thresholds, guess a fact only the researcher knows, retry an unknown failure, or publish private run data. Harness development. The harness records each runner invocation, including its output, before and after state, return status, and an index of pipeline logs. An opt-in hook also retains the agent’s transcripts locally. These records support a development workflow for the harness itself. GEPA proposes and evaluates prompt changes from execution feedback, while ACE separates generation, reflection, and curation of reusable context [Agrawal et al., 2025, Zhang et al., 2025]. Our workflow is simpler.

The agent selects local records, describes a problem that can be reproduced and proposes one small change. A script runs the changed and unchanged harness on the same records, and a change that passes goes to maintainer review. Evaluating this workflow on independent screens, and adopting a full optimizer such as GEPA, are promising future directions. F Reanalysis of existing screens All five reanalyses ran through every module to clustering, and no quality gate was overridden by hand. Usable cells. We re-ran five screens previously analyzed by hand (denali, kilimanjaro, mayon, jebel, shasta) end to end with the harness on cloud virtual machines, producing damavand, kazbek, matterhorn, jannu and snowdon respectively. We compared the number of usable cells, defined as cells with a confident single-gene assignment at the end of merge. That count rose in all five pairs from the same raw images, by 3.8, 4.4, 23.4, 39.2 and 20.6 percent (Figure 2, Table 1). As a share of the cells entering aggregation, usable cells rose in four of the five pairs, for example from 48.1 to 59.2 percent on kazbek and from 41.1 to 54.3 percent on matterhorn. On jannu the share fell slightly, from 52.8 to 51.3 percent, because 7.9 percent more cells entered merge in the harness run. The SBS mapping rate, which both analyses recorded for only two pairs, also rose, by 2.4 percentage points on damavand and 11.6 on kazbek. All numbers are read from each run’s own evaluation outputs, so both analyses are measured the same way. The harness also replaced hand-set round values with measured ones, for example nuclei and cell diameters of 13.97 and 42.14 pixels in place of 15 and 45 on one screen. Researcher effort. Each screen’s interview resolves 212 notebook parameters. On damavand and jannu, the two reanalyses whose interview records survive, the researcher was asked 6 and 9 questions and supplied 14 and 12 values in total (Figure 5).

The remaining values came from the screen description, lab defaults, data probes, or parameter sweeps. G Extending Brieflow to a drug screen Table 2 lists the changes to Brieflow that came from running the harness on the drug screen of Section 4.3, grouped by what each change addressed. Each fix entered the pipeline itself, so every later screen benefits from it. Microscope format. The extension screen was imaged on an Opera Phenix.

Preprocess failed at the first stage, and the harness classified the failure as a configuration mismatch and reported the failing step and its error message. The fix was a file-type metadata reader in the pipeline (#246) and a matching harness release that probes the format automatically. The resumed run then failed one stage later on an empty per-cycle metadata table (#248), then on well identifiers the tile selector could not split (#249). Further fixes in the same family followed as later stages encountered the same well names. One of them raised no error at all: per-well segmentation summaries silently summed each plate column (#257), which an audit of the quality outputs caught. Drug screen. The same screen identifies constructs rather than knockouts and compares each construct under treatment with its untreated arm. Brieflow’s aggregation and clustering assume knockouts scored against non-targeting controls within one treatment, so four parts of the pipeline were extended. The two-color chemistry needed a combinatorial base caller (#242). The phenotype stage needed features defined by the screen, and aggregation needed construct identities grouped by treatment with the null distribution drawn from the untreated arm (#258). Scoring then needed each construct compared with its own untreated arm rather than with a control construct (#293). Segmentation, barcode mapping, and merge ran unchanged, and each new parameter entered the screen repository’s notebooks. Every change is reviewed and keeps existing screens working, so Brieflow serves drug screens of barcoded constructs as well as knockout screens.

H Portability The harness can be adapted to other pipelines that are divided into modules, where each module has configurable inputs, a way to run it, a signal that it has finished, a way to resume after a failure, and outputs that can be checked for quality. Brieflow and Snakemake provide these here. The porting guide released with the harness (HARNESS.md) divides the harness code into three parts. The first can be reused without changes: the list of modules, the loop that configures, validates, runs, and checks each module, the job monitor, and the connections to each compute scheduler. The second must be rewritten for a new pipeline: how a module is configured (here, a marimo notebook), how failures are read from logs, and the checks before and after each module runs. The third is policy that each group sets from its own experience: how much to raise memory after a failure, how long to wait on a slow filesystem, and the quality thresholds that define a passing result. 10
